body: On a Sunday morning in a hall with a low ceiling, a woman of eighty-one stands in the third row with her handbag still over her arm. The band is four songs in and she has not sung any of them. It is not the volume; she was in a choir for forty years and volume has never bothered her. She is waiting for the beat to come round to where she can step into it, the way you wait at a kerb for a gap in traffic, and it does not come. Twice she lifts her hand and puts it down again. At the end of the fourth song she sits, folds her hands, looks perfectly content, and does not stand up again.
She was not being difficult and she was not disapproving. She could not find the door. Everybody else in the room was inside a thing she was standing next to.

There is a useful test for any church music and it costs nothing to apply. Could your grandmother find her way into this. Not enjoy it, necessarily, and certainly not choose it — but recognise it. Find the beat. Know where the line lands and when to come in.

It is worth taking the word recognise literally, because it is doing precise work and it is not a word about taste. Rhythm is learned early and learned in the body. A person who grew up clapping on a particular beat will find it in almost anything, anticipate it slightly, and feel a small physical satisfaction when it arrives where they expected. That capacity survives deafness in the higher registers, it survives dementia further than almost anything else, and it is why a woman who cannot remember a grandchild’s name comes in exactly on time on the second line of a hymn. What it does not survive is a pulse it cannot locate. You can follow a rhythm you dislike. You cannot follow one you cannot find.

This dial carries 121 stations between HM 300.30 and HM 398.70, 46 of them on air, sorted by form rather than by how recent anything is. Hymns, gospel, country, rap and Afro-Caribbean fusion each hold a frequency.

Sorting a band that way is more expensive than the alternative and there is a reason it is done. The cheap arrangement is one contemporary blend on every frequency, because that is what the largest number of people will tolerate at any moment. The dear arrangement keeps older forms in permanent rotation on numbers that never move, including forms that will never be anybody’s idea of current. That is a deliberate purchase, and it buys one guarantee: if your grandmother could not find her way into it, something got replaced rather than developed.

The thing being guarded against is not novelty. It is a very particular kind of import. Over the last few decades one style of worship — a good style, well made, sincerely meant — has been exported from a handful of countries to more or less everywhere, along with the equipment, the lighting and the running order. A congregation in Lagos, in Manila and in Manchester can now sound like the same room, and the room is in none of those cities. Nobody imposed it. It arrived on the strength of being available, and filled the space where a local form had been developing on its own.

Which is where development has to be told apart from replacement, and the distinction is not sentimental. Development moves and stays legible to the people it came from: the tempo changes, the instruments change, somebody adds a bridge, and the grandmother still finds the beat because it is descended from the one she learned. Replacement imports a whole form from elsewhere, and its tell is exactly the scene in the third row. The previous generation is not being challenged by it. They are locked out of it, in their own church, using a shape that arrived from a country none of them have been to.
So the question is not whether the music has changed. It is whether it changed from something, or was swapped for something.

The opposite case deserves a proper hearing, because it is strong. Young people should not be made to worship inside 1968 out of respect for people who will not be there in ten years. Traditions that stop moving become museum pieces within a generation, and a church that sounds like a preservation society will be preserved exactly like one, with nobody in it. All of that is true, and none of it is what happens when a form is imported wholesale. Development costs a congregation something: it takes musicians who know the older repertoire well enough to move it. Replacement costs nothing but a subscription and a screen, which is why it wins so often, and why a church that takes it will have to take it again in fifteen years, with nothing of its own left to develop from.
A tradition that fails the grandmother test did not grow. It was substituted.

There is a front room in Birmingham where a boy of seventeen is showing his grandmother something on his phone, mostly to be kind, because she asked what he listens to and he does not think she will get far with it. It is a gospel track with a bit of dancehall underneath and a chorus about the same thing his church has sung about for a hundred years. Four bars in, her hand starts going on the offbeat — not the beat, the offbeat, without hesitation and without looking at anything. She learned that in a yard in Kingston when she was fourteen and has never once had to think about it since. He watches her hand for a moment and says nothing, and later that week he plays her another one.

That is what a rhythm your grandmother knows actually looks like in practice. Nothing was explained, nothing was conceded, and neither of them changed their taste. The music had simply been developed from something she already had in her hands.

It costs something to hold that line and the cost is not small. A station that keeps older forms in rotation will sound dated to a nineteen-year-old, and dated is no small problem when he has an entire industry offering him something that sounds like this month. Some old forms genuinely are worse — sentimental, thinly written, badly recorded — and continuity is no argument for keeping bad songs. Worse, the test can be misused by anybody who dislikes change and wants a principle to hide behind.

But the discomfort is the point rather than a fault in it. A form everybody in the building finds immediately comfortable has stopped doing anything, and a form nobody over sixty can enter has quietly told half a congregation that their part is over. Sitting between the two is uncomfortable by design. It means the band has to play something the young find slightly old and the old find slightly fast, which is exactly the condition a tradition is in while it is still alive.

So continuity is not conservatism, and it is not nostalgia either. It is the test of whether a thing was ever really yours. A form you developed will always have somewhere in it your grandmother can stand. A form you imported will not, and no amount of good intention or excellent musicianship puts one there afterwards.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

The band carries four kinds of programming and it is worth knowing they are there before you start turning. There is music, which is most of it — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, safe to leave running in a room with children in it. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. Every format holds a permanent number, so a form does not lose its place on the dial when it stops being fashionable.

If you want to hear development rather than replacement, start at HM 311.50 — Riddim and Rhyme. It is the Afro-Caribbean frequency on this band, and it is the right one for this argument because of what it is made of: reggae, dancehall, soca and Afrobeats married to teaching hymnody and gospel-soul — a set of rhythms people inherited joined to a body of words people inherited. Nothing about it was imported wholesale. Zariah Inspire hosts it, Morning Riddim runs early and the Yard Session at night, and it will play a grandmother a pulse she has had in her hands since she was fourteen underneath a chorus her church has sung for a century. That is what passing the test sounds like when somebody has done the work.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. Add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which forms people are actually reaching for — which is how the next frequency, and the next generation of a form, get built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. Put HM 311.50 on in a room with somebody thirty years older than you in it, on an ordinary afternoon, and then do not explain it and do not apologise for it. Watch their hands. If they find the beat inside four bars, you are listening to something developed rather than swapped, and you will have learned more in those four bars than any argument about worship styles has ever settled.
